concept.name: Creek
concept.definition: A Wyckoff metaphor, coined by teacher Robert Evans, for the zone of resistance at the upper boundary of an accumulation trading range — the 'creek' that price must jump across to begin markup. It is informal terminology for resistance, not a distinct technical pattern.
concept.intuition: Resistance is pictured as a stream of sellers; the market has to gather enough strength to leap over it.
concept.mechanics: The creek level is approximated by the highs of rallies within the accumulation range (often the automatic-rally high and later upthrusts). A decisive advance through it on widening spread and volume is a 'jump across the creek' (SOS); a subsequent low-volume pullback to the creek area is a 'back-up to the creek'.
relationships: Backup to the edge of the creek
concept.failure_modes: Because the creek is a zone rather than a precise line, analysts disagree on its placement; failed jumps that fall back into the range show the level was misjudged or demand insufficient.
concept.misconceptions: The creek is a teaching metaphor, not a Wyckoff event with formal rules; it appears in the Evans/Pruden tradition rather than in Wyckoff's original course terminology.
concept.example: An analyst marks the 100-102 zone, where three rallies died inside a base, as the creek; when price later clears 103 on heavy volume, she calls it a jump across the creek.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
